title: Sliding Window Maximum
prompt:
You are given an array of integers `nums` and a window size `k`. A window of size `k` slides from the left of the array to the right, one position at a time. For every position of the window, report the maximum value inside it.

This powers a real-time dashboard that shows the peak request latency over the last `k` samples, so it must handle very large streams efficiently.
inputFormat: Line 1: n k. Line 2: n space-separated integers.
outputFormat: n-k+1 space-separated integers: the maximum of each window, left to right.
referenceNotes: Optimal: monotonic decreasing deque of indices; pop back while smaller-or-equal, pop front when out of window. Each index pushed/popped once -> O(n). Traps: O(nk) brute force; heap without lazy deletion (O(n log n) but OK-ish); using list.pop(0) / array.shift() for the queue -> O(n) per pop; storing values instead of indices breaks expiry with duplicates; off-by-one when emitting (i >= k-1). Probe ideas: why a deque over a heap, what if k changes per query, streaming input that doesn't fit in memory, amortized analysis argument.

starterCode.PYTHON:
from __future__ import annotations

import sys

def max_sliding_window(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    # Return the maximum of every contiguous window of size k.

    return result


def main() -> None:
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    n, k = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
    nums = [int(x) for x in data[2:2 + n]]
    print(" ".join(map(str, max_sliding_window(nums, k))))

title: Course Schedule (Lexicographic Order)
prompt:
A university has `n` courses labelled `0..n-1`. Some courses have prerequisites: a pair `(a, b)` means course `b` must be completed before course `a`.

Return an order in which a student can take every course. If several valid orders exist, return the **lexicographically smallest** one. If it is impossible to finish all courses, output `IMPOSSIBLE`.
inputFormat: Line 1: n m. Next m lines: a b (b is a prerequisite of a).
outputFormat: n space-separated course ids, or the word IMPOSSIBLE.
constraints: pairs may repeat; self-loops are possible
referenceNotes: Optimal: Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap instead of a FIFO queue -> O((n+m) log n). DFS-based topo sort does NOT give the lexicographically smallest order. Traps: plain BFS queue gives a valid but not smallest order; duplicate edges double-counted in indegree are fine only if decremented the same number of times; self-loop must yield IMPOSSIBLE; recursion depth with DFS on a 20000-chain. Probe ideas: why a heap, why DFS post-order fails here, cycle detection proof (processed count < n), what if prerequisites arrive as a stream.

title: Merge Overlapping Reservations
prompt:
A booking system stores reservations as closed intervals `[start, end]`. Two reservations that overlap **or touch** (e.g. `[1,4]` and `[4,5]`) must be merged into one block.

Given all reservations in arbitrary order, output the merged blocks sorted by start time.
inputFormat: Line 1: n. Next n lines: start end.
outputFormat: One merged interval per line: start end, sorted by start.
referenceNotes: Optimal: sort by start, single sweep extending the last block's end with max(). O(n log n). Traps: forgetting max() for nested intervals ([1,10],[2,3]); using < instead of <= for touching; 32-bit overflow in Java/C++ with values up to 2e9 (int overflow!); O(n^2) repeated merging. Probe ideas: overflow on line reading ends, can it be O(n) if values are bounded (counting/bucket), streaming insert of a new interval (balanced BST / interval tree), stability of sort irrelevant.

title: Network Delay Time
prompt:
A network has `n` nodes labelled `1..n` and `m` directed links. A link `(u, v, w)` means a signal takes `w` milliseconds to travel from `u` to `v`.

A signal is sent from node `src`. Return the time it takes for **all** nodes to receive it, or `-1` if some node can never receive it.
inputFormat: Line 1: n m src. Next m lines: u v w.
referenceNotes: Optimal: Dijkstra with a binary heap and lazy deletion (skip stale entries) -> O((n+m) log n). Traps: Bellman-Ford O(nm) times out on the large case; BFS ignoring weights; forgetting the stale-entry check (still correct but slower); visiting node marked on push instead of pop gives wrong answers; unreachable detection. Probe ideas: why Dijkstra fails with negative weights, decrease-key vs lazy deletion trade-off, dense graph -> O(n^2) array version, 0-1 BFS when weights are 0/1.
